## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta* (DN 4) is set at Campā, the capital of Aṅga, whose revenues had been granted by King Bimbisāra to the prominent brāhmaṇa Soṇadaṇḍa [Rhys Davids & Oldenberg; Pande 1974]. When Soṇadaṇḍa prepares to visit the Buddha despite other brahmins protesting that doing so is beneath his stature, they praise his distinguished pedigree and mastery of bodily marks (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), while the sutta also records the belief that the Buddha's presence protects communities from harm by non-humans [Anālayo 2017; Holz; Pande 1974]. In the subsequent dialogue, the Buddha reframes caste identity into ethical terms, showing that a true brahmin is defined by moral character and conduct rather than birth or caste status [Hubbard & Swanson 1997; Keown 1992].

Under the Buddha's questioning, Soṇadaṇḍa reduces the indispensable qualities of a true brahmin to virtue (*sīla*) and wisdom (*paññā*), illustrating their mutual dependence with the simile of one hand washing the other or one foot washing the other [Keown 1992]. In this twofold path structure, the meditative absorptions and higher attainments are subsumed under wisdom (*paññā*), while the commentary notes that Soṇadaṇḍa had only the five lay precepts in mind whereas the Buddha intended the full monastic path [Gombrich 1984; Keown 1992]. Scholars note that DN 4 builds upon the foundational framework of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) while notably avoiding miracles and mythical elements [Kingsbury 2002; Pande 1974].

The discourse has a direct Chinese parallel in the *Dīrgha-āgama* (DĀ 22, *Zhongde jing* 種德經), and corresponding Sanskrit manuscript fragments are preserved (SHT sutta56 and SF 42) [Dhammajoti 2015; Martin 2006]. DharmaNexus matches confirm this alignment with DĀ 22 (T 1.15) and reveal extensive Pali-internal text reuse, particularly with the *Kūṭadanta Sutta* (DN 5, especially §4.2–7.1) and the *Caṅkī Sutta* (MN 95, §5.4–6.24), in addition to shared formulas across the Vinaya *Khandhakas* and the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* [DharmaNexus].
